title: Git Pack Files
description: Understand how Git pack files work, how delta compression saves space, and how to inspect pack contents.

data.text: As a repository grows, Git consolidates loose objects into pack files for efficiency. Pack files store multiple objects in a single file and use delta compression to avoid storing duplicate data. Understanding pack files helps you diagnose slow clones and large repository sizes.

New objects are stored as loose files — one file per object in a two-level directory structure. As the number of loose objects grows, Git automatically runs git gc and repacks them into pack files. Pack files are more space-efficient and faster to download.

data.title: Loose vs packed
items: **Loose**: One file per object, fast to write, slower to read at scale
**Packed**: Multiple objects in one file, uses delta compression, faster overall for large repos
Git automatically transitions loose objects to pack files via git gc
Pack files live in .git/objects/pack/ and end with .pack

data.title: Inspect pack files and delta compression
data.code:
# List all pack files
tree .git/objects/pack/

# Verify pack file integrity
git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/pack-*.idx | head -20

# Count objects in pack files vs loose
git count-objects -v

# Repack manually
git repack -a -d --depth=250 --window=250

data.text: Delta compression stores objects as changes against a base object. When two files are similar (like a file modified across commits), Git stores only the delta and the base, not two full copies. The --depth and --window options to git repack control how aggressively Git searches for deltas.

data.title: Trade-off: CPU vs disk
data.text: Aggressive delta compression (large --depth and --window) uses more CPU during repack but produces smaller pack files. The default settings balance both. Use --aggressive only during maintenance windows.

Modern Git (2.20+) supports multi-pack index (MIDX) files that merge information from multiple pack files into a single index. This improves performance for repositories with many pack files. Git manages MIDX automatically during git gc.

data.title: Enable and inspect MIDX
data.code:
# Enable multi-pack index
git config --local pack.useMultiPackIndex true

# Run gc to build the MIDX
git gc

# List pack files and MIDX files
tree .git/objects/pack/

# Verify MIDX is in use
git count-objects -v
# Look for 'multi-pack-index: 1' in the output

data.title: Pack files and network transfer
data.text: When you clone or fetch, Git transfers objects in pack files over the wire. A well-packed repository clones faster and uses less bandwidth, which matters significantly for CI pipelines and developer onboarding.

items.question: Can I transfer pack files manually?
items.answer: Yes, using git bundle. A bundle is a single file containing a pack plus refs, suitable for offline transfer. Use git bundle create repo.bundle --all to create one.

items.question: Will repacking break my repository?
items.answer: No. git repack always preserves all objects and creates new pack files atomically. The old loose objects are removed only after the pack is verified.

items.question: Why is my pack file larger than the loose objects?
items.answer: Pack files include metadata and index files. The .pack file stores the raw objects; the .idx file stores the index. Both together are usually slightly larger than loose objects before optimization, but they compress better over time.

items.question: What triggers git gc automatically?
items.answer: Git runs gc when loose objects exceed gc.auto (default 6700), when there are too many pack files, or during certain commands like git commit and git merge.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Pack files consolidate multiple objects into a single file for efficiency
Delta compression stores objects as changes against a base to save space
git gc and git repack manage the transition from loose to packed
Multi-pack index (MIDX) improves performance for repos with many pack files
Well-packed repositories clone faster and use less disk space
